title.en: Nitetis and the Child's Vow: The Above Made Below
title.zh: 奈提提斯與童誓言：以上為下

region.en: Persia and Egypt (the disputed princess whose double marriage brought the conquest)
region.zh: 波斯與埃及（雙重身世的公主招致征服）

texts.period: Persian-Egyptian tale recorded by Herodotus, Histories III.1-3 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book III, secs. 1-3

summary.en: Amasis, fearing Cambyses would wed him to his own daughter, sent him the only daughter of Apries instead, dressed as his own — until Cambyses called her by the wrong father's name and she told the truth; the Persians say this began the invasion, while the Egyptians make the reverse claim; and the boy Cambyses, hearing his mother scorned, vowed: 'I will make that which is above in Egypt to be below, and that which is below above.'
summary.zh: 阿馬西斯恐岡比西斯索其女為妻，遂以阿普里埃斯之獨女盛裝冒充己女送之——及岡比西斯誤喚其父名，公主道破真相；波斯人謂此即侵略之因，埃及人則反稱其血緣；童年的岡比西斯聞母受辱，誓曰：『我必使埃及之上者為下、下者為上。』

sensitivity.note: Ancient historical-legendary tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: There was a daughter of Apries the former king, very tall and comely of form and the only person left of his house, and her name was Nitetis. This girl Amasis adorned with raiment and with gold, and sent her away to Persia as his own daughter: but after a time, when Cambyses saluted her calling her by the name of her father, the girl said to him: 'O king, thou dost not perceive how thou hast been deceived by Amasis; for he adorned me with ornaments and sent me away giving me to thee as his own daughter, whereas in truth I am the daughter of Apries against whom Amasis rose up with the Egyptians and murdered him, who was his lord and master.' These words uttered and this occasion having arisen, led Cambyses the son of Cyrus against Egypt, moved to very great anger.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book III.1.

passages.text: Cassandane, who was the wife of Cyrus, spoke as follows: 'Nevertheless, though I am the mother of such children of these, Cyrus treats me with dishonour and holds in honour her whom he has brought in from Egypt.' Thus she spoke, they say, being vexed by Nitetis, and upon that Cambyses the elder of her sons said: 'For this cause, mother, when I am grown to be a man, I will make that which is above in Egypt to be below, and that which is below above.' This he is reported to have said when he was perhaps about ten years old, and the women were astonished by it: and he, they say, kept it ever in mind, and so at last when he had become a man and had obtained the royal power, he made the expedition against Egypt.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book III.3.

title.en: Psammenitos at the Water-carriers: The Wise King's Tears
title.zh: 普薩美尼托斯與汲水者：智者之淚

region.en: Memphis, suburb of the city (the captive king seated before Cambyses)
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯城郊（被俘之王坐於岡比西斯之前）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories III.14-15 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book III, secs. 14-15

summary.en: Cambyses leads the daughter of Psammenitos in slave's dress to draw water, his son to execution — and the deposed king only bows to the earth; but when an aged beggar of his own company passes, begging from the soldiers, Psammenitos weeps aloud: 'My own troubles were too great for me to lament them aloud, but the trouble of my companion was such as called for tears' — and Croesus wept too.
summary.zh: 岡比西斯使普薩美尼托斯之女著奴衣汲水，其子縛索牽往就刑——亡王僅俯身向地；及一窮老同僚乞食而過，王乃放聲大哭：『我自身之苦，過於我所能哭；而吾友之苦，堪當一哭』——居魯士亦為之泣。

sensitivity.note: Ancient moral tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: Cambyses sent his daughter with the other maidens, dressed as was the daughter of the king: and as the maidens were passing by their fathers with cries and lamentation, the other men all began to cry out and lament aloud, seeing that their children had been evilly entreated, but Psammenitos when he saw it before his eyes and perceived it bent himself down to the earth. Then when the water-bearers had passed by, next Cambyses sent his son with two thousand Egyptians besides who were of the same age, with ropes bound round their necks and bits placed in their mouths; and these were being led away to execution.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book III.14.

passages.text: When these also had passed by, it chanced that a man of his table companions, advanced in years, who had been deprived of all his possessions and had nothing except such things as a beggar possesses, and was asking alms from the soldiers, passed by Psammenitos the son of Amasis and the Egyptians who were sitting in the suburb of the city: and when Psammenitos saw him he uttered a great cry of lamentation, and he called his companion by name and beat himself upon the head. — Cambyses marvelled at that which he did, and he sent a messenger and asked him: 'Psammenitos, thy master Cambyses asks thee for what reason, when thou sawest thy daughter evilly entreated and thy son going to death, thou didst not cry aloud nor lament for them, whereas thou didst honour with these signs of grief the beggar who, as he hears from others, is not in any way related to thee?'
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book III.14.

passages.text: The other answered as follows: 'O son of Cyrus, my own troubles were too great for me to lament them aloud, but the trouble of my companion was such as called for tears, seeing that he has been deprived of great wealth, and has come to beggary upon the threshold of old age.' When this saying was reported by the messenger, it seemed to them that it was well spoken; and, as is reported by the Egyptians, Croesus shed tears (for he also, as fortune would have it, had accompanied Cambyses to Egypt) and the Persians who were present shed tears also; and there entered some pity into Cambyses himself, and forthwith he bade them save the life of the son of Psammenitos.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book III.14.

title.en: The Body of Amasis: The Oracle and the Substitute Corpse
title.zh: 阿馬西斯之身：神諭與替身屍

region.en: Sais, Egypt (the burial-place in the temple, near the doors)
region.zh: 埃及薩伊斯（神廟內之葬室，近門處）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories III.16 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book III, sec. 16

summary.en: Cambyses enters the palace of Amasis, drags out the embalmed king, has him scourged, plucked and stabbed — but the Egyptians say it was not Amasis at all: the king had learned from an oracle what would befall his body after death, buried a double of his own stature near the doors, and enjoined his son to lay his own body in the innermost recess; Herodotus half doubts, as 'pride and no good ground.'
summary.zh: 岡比西斯入阿馬西斯王宮，拖出其木乃伊鞭笞拔毛穿刺——而埃及人言：彼非阿馬西斯！王生前自神諭得知死後之事，遂以一身材相同者代葬於門側，並囑其子將己身安置室中最深之處。希羅多德半信半疑，謂此乃『出於驕矜而無實據』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions.

passages.text: From Memphis Cambyses came to the city of Sais with the purpose of doing that which in fact he did: for when he had entered into the palace of Amasis, he forthwith gave command to bring the corpse of Amasis forth out of his burial-place; and when this had been accomplished, he gave command to scourge it and pluck out the hair and stab it, and to do to it dishonour in every possible way besides: and when they had done this too until they were wearied out, for the corpse being embalmed held out against the violence and did not fall to pieces in any part, Cambyses gave command to consume it with fire, enjoining thereby a thing which was not permitted by religion.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book III.16.

passages.text: However, the Egyptians say that it was not Amasis who suffered this outrage, but another of the Egyptians who was of the same stature of body as Amasis; and that to him the Persians did outrage, thinking that they were doing it to Amasis: for they say that Amasis learnt from an Oracle that which was about to happen with regard to himself after his death; and accordingly, to avert the evil which threatened to come upon him, he buried the dead body of this man who was scourged within his own sepulchral chamber near the doors, and enjoined his son to lay his own body as much as possible in the inner recess of the chamber. These injunctions, said to have been given by Amasis with regard to his burial and with regard to the man mentioned, were not in my opinion really given at all, but I think that the Egyptians make pretence of it from pride and with no good ground.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book III.16.

title.en: Cambyses Stabs the Apis: The Mad King and the Dying God
title.zh: 岡比西斯刺阿匹斯：狂王與垂死之神

region.en: Memphis, Egypt (the temple where Apis lay dying of his wound)
region.zh: 埃及孟菲斯（阿匹斯負傷垂死之神廟）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories III.27-30 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book III, secs. 27-30

summary.en: Apis appears and Egypt wears its fairest garments; Cambyses, assuming mockery of his failures, kills the officers, summons the god — and finds a calf 'black, with a white square on the forehead, the likeness of an eagle on its back, double hairs in the tail, and a mark like a beetle on the tongue,' born of a cow that a flash of light from heaven has struck. Drawing his dagger he stabs the calf in the thigh and laughs: 'Are gods born such as this, with blood and flesh, and sensible of the stroke of iron weapons?' — and straightway, the Egyptians say, he went mad.
summary.zh: 阿匹斯顯現，埃及人皆著盛裝慶賀；岡比西斯以為譏己之敗，誅官吏，召神入前——所見乃一黑犢：額有白方、背如鷹形、尾毛雙生、舌上若有甲蟲之印，乃天光下注之母牛所生。王拔匕首刺其股而笑曰：『神而生而有血肉、能覺鐵器之傷者，如此而已乎？』——埃及人謂其自此而狂。

sensitivity.note: Ancient king-atrocity tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Pairs with the Ochus-apis record cut from Plutarch.

passages.text: When Cambyses arrived at Memphis, Apis appeared to the Egyptians, whom the Hellenes call Epaphos: and when he had appeared, forthwith the Egyptians began to wear their fairest garments and to have festivities. Cambyses accordingly seeing the Egyptians doing thus, and supposing that they were certainly acting so by way of rejoicing because he had fared ill, called for the officers who had charge of Memphis... They said that a god had appeared to them, who was wont to appear at intervals of long time, and that whenever he appeared, then all the Egyptians rejoiced and kept festival. Hearing this Cambyses said that they were lying, and as liars he condemned them to death.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book III.27.

passages.text: This Apis-Epaphos is a calf born of a cow who after this is not permitted to conceive any other offspring; and the Egyptians say that a flash of light comes down from heaven upon this cow, and of this she produces Apis. This calf which is called Apis is black and has the following signs, namely a white square upon the forehead, and on the back the likeness of an eagle, and in the tail the hairs are double, and on the tongue there is a mark like a beetle.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book III.28.

passages.text: When the priests had brought Apis, Cambyses being somewhat affected with madness drew his dagger, and aiming at the belly of Apis, struck his thigh: then he laughed and said to the priests: 'O ye wretched creatures, are gods born such as this, with blood and flesh, and sensible of the stroke of iron weapons? Worthy indeed of Egyptians is such a god as this. Ye however at least shall not escape without punishment for making a mock of me.'... Apis wounded by the stroke in his thigh lay dying in the temple. Him, when he had brought his life to an end by reason of the wound, the priests buried without the knowledge of Cambyses: but Cambyses, as the Egyptians say, immediately after this evil deed became absolutely mad, not having been really in his right senses even before that time.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book III.29-30.

title.en: The Fifty Thousand Who Vanished in the Sand
title.zh: 消失於黃沙的五萬大軍

region.en: The desert between the Oasis (the Isle of the Blessed) and the Oracle of Ammon (symbolic pin over the Libyan sand sea)
region.zh: 祝福之島與阿蒙神諭之間的利比亞沙海（象徵定位）

texts.period: Recorded by Herodotus, Histories III.25-26 (5th century BCE; Macaulay translation 1890)

source.work: The History of Herodotus, trans. G. C. Macaulay (1890), Book III, secs. 25-26

summary.en: Cambyses sent fifty thousand men from Thebes to enslave the Ammonians and burn the oracle of Zeus; they reached the Oasis — the Greeks' Isle of the Blessed — and from there, says the whole world, nothing: the Ammonians themselves tell that at their morning meal, mid-way through the sand, a violent south wind arose and buried the army under heaps of desert sand, 'and so they disappeared and were seen no more.'
summary.zh: 岡比西斯自底比斯遣五萬眾，欲奴役阿蒙人、焚宙斯神諭之座；軍至綠洲——即希臘人所謂『祝福之島』——此後天下無人能言其蹤：阿蒙人自述，正午餐之際，南風驟起，挾沙如山，盡埋其軍，『自此不復得見』。

sensitivity.note: Ancient marvel-tale via Herodotus; no living community restrictions. Tagged 'otherworld-voyage' for the vanishing-into-the-otherworld reading; recorded as an interpretive choice.

passages.text: When in the course of his march he had arrived at Thebes, he divided off about fifty thousand of his army, and these he enjoined to make slaves of the Ammonians and to set fire to the seat of the Oracle of Zeus, but he himself with the remainder of his army went on against the Ethiopians.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay, Herodotus (1890), Book III.25.

passages.text: Those of the Persians who had been sent to march against the Ammonians set forth from Thebes and went on their way with guides; and it is known that they arrived at the city of Oasis, which is inhabited by Samians said to be of the Aischrionian tribe, and is distant seven days' journey from Thebes over sandy desert: now this place is called in the speech of the Hellenes the 'Isle of the Blessed.' It is said that the army reached this place, but from that point onwards, except the Ammonians themselves and those who have heard the account from them, no man is able to say anything about them; for they neither reached the Ammonians nor returned back.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book III.26.

passages.text: This however is added to the story by the Ammonians themselves: — they say that as the army was going from this Oasis through the sandy desert to attack them, and had got to a point about mid-way between them and the Oasis, while they were taking their morning meal a violent South Wind blew upon them, and bearing with it heaps of the desert sand it buried them under it, and so they disappeared and were seen no more. Thus the Ammonians say that it came to pass with regard to this army.
passages.note: Verbatim excerpt of Macaulay (1890), Book III.26.
